metadata.title: United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321 (1998) (No. 96-1487)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: United States v. Bajakajian

Opinion filed: 1998-06-22

Docket No.: 96-1487

Citations:
• 141 L. Ed. 2d 314
• 118 S. Ct. 2028
• 524 U.S. 321
• 1998 U.S. LEXIS 4172

Case holding summaries:
• distinguishing cases directed against "guilty property" and noting that "[t]raditional in rem forfeitures were . . . not considered punishment against the individual for an offense"
• "Historically, the conduct of the property owner [in an in rem proceeding] was irrelevant; indeed the owner of forfeited property could be entirely innocent of any crime."
• “The text and history of the Excessive Fines Clause demonstrate the centrality of proportionality to the excessiveness inquiry . . . .”
• stating that "judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature"
• "[M]odern statutory forfeiture is a `fine' for Eighth Amendment purposes if it constitutes punishment even in part, regardless of whether the proceeding is styled in rem or in personam."
• holding that forfeiture 70 times the Guidelines maximum and greater than the statutory maximum would be unconstitutionally excessive
• stating that “judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature”
• requiring, for purposes of an excessive fines issue, that a proportionality analysis be conducted, assessing whether "the amount of the forfeiture is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the defendant's offense"
• explaining that the monetary penalty at issue in One Lot Emerald Cut Stones was remedial in part because made for the first time in reply briefs
• “[J]udgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature. . . . [A]ny judicial determination regarding the gravity of a particular criminal offense will be inherently imprecise.”
• contemplating the harm “caused by a hypothetical drug dealer who willfully fails to report taking $12,000 out of the country in order to purchase drugs”
• holding that a forfeiture of $357,144 was excessive where the maximum fine under the Sentencing Guidelines was $5,000
• “Excessive means surpassing the usual, the proper, or a normal measure of proportion.”
• “Excessive means surpassing the usual, the proper, or a normal measure of proportion.”
• "Although in personam criminal forfeitures were well established in England at the time of the founding, they were rejected altogether in the laws of this country until very recently."
• despite differing facts emphasized by the majority and dissent, the majority held that “Respondent’s crime was solely a reporting offense”
• distinguishing punitive in personam forfeiture from remedial in rem forfeiture
• holding unconstitutionally excessive a similar forfeiture of currency that defendant was carrying out of U.S. without reporting, an offense not connected to other wrongdoing
• explaining that a fine is unconstitutionally excessive under the Eighth Amendment if its amount is grossly disproportionate to the gravity of the offense
• holding that punitive forfeiture will violate the Excessive Fines Clause if "grossly disproportional" to the gravity of the offense
• "[A] punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant's offense."
• “‘[R]emedial action’ is one ‘brought to obtain compensation or indemnity[.]’” (first alteration in original) (quoting Remedial action, Black’s Law Dictionary (6th ed. 1990))
• “Historically, . . . the owner of forfeited property could be entirely innocent of any crime.”
• “[In personam] forfeitures have historically been treated as punitive, being part of the punishment imposed for felonies and treason in the Middle Ages and at common law.”
• “Because the forfeiture of respondent’s currency constitutes . . . a ‘fine’ within the meaning of the Excessive Fines Clause, we now turn to the question whether it is ‘excessive.’”
• explaining that the Clause “limits the government’s power to extract payments” from an individual
• stating that excessive means surpassing the usual, the proper or a normal measure of proportion
• goods unladen without a permit
• holding falsehoods on customs forms justify forfeiture even if the lies do not affect the duties due and paid
• "Whatever views may be entertained regarding severity of punishment, . . . these are peculiarly questions of legislative policy"
• "[I]t is the property which is proceeded against, and, by resort to a legal fiction, held guilty and condemned as though it were conscious instead of inanimate and insentient"
• "Reviewing courts . . . should grant substantial deference to the broad authority that legislatures necessarily possess in determining the types and limits of punishments for crimes"
• noting Court of Appeals' statement that "`the government is exacting too high a penalty in relation to the offense committed' "
• customs statute requiring the forfeiture of undeclared goods concealed in baggage and imposing a monetary penalty equal to the value of the goods imposed a "remedial, rather than [a] punitive sanctio[n]"
• "It is in the light of the extensive criminal activities which petitioner apparently conducted . . . that the question whether the forfeiture was `excessive' must be considered"
• "Instrumentalities historically have been treated as a form of 'guilty property' that can be forfeited in civil in rem proceedings."
• holding substantial deference should be given to legislature in determining whether fine is excessive in violation of Eighth 2 Amendment of United States Constitution
• "The factual findings made by the district courts in conducting the excessive[ ] [fines] inquiry, of course, must be accepted unless clearly erroneous."
• stating that "forfeiture of the currency here does not serve the remedial purpose of compensating the Government for a loss"
• requiring, for purposes of an excessive fines issue, that a proportionality analysis be conducted, assessing whether "the amount of the forfeiture is grossly dispropor- tional to the gravity of the defendant’s offense"
• noting that while traditionally civil forfeitures were considered non-punitive, "it does not follow, of course, that all modern civil in rem forfeitures are non- punitive and thus beyond the coverage of the excessive fines clause."
• holding that forfeiture of currency for violating 31 U.S.C. § 5316(a)(1)(A)—a statute requiring persons to report when transporting more than $10,000 outside of the United States—constitutes a fine within the meaning of the Excessive Page 24 of 28 Fines Clause
• “[D]espite the differences between restitution and a traditional fine, restitution still implicates the prosecutorial powers of government[.]”
• “[J]udgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature.”
• “[J]udgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature.”
• holding that "a punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant's offense"
• noting that "judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature"
• stating that one “particularly relevant” consideration in deriving a standard for constitutional excessiveness is “that judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature”
• concluding that a fine is remedial when it compensates the government for a loss
• "It was only in 1970 that Congress resurrected the English common law of punitive forfeiture to combat organized crime and major drug trafficking."
